q: In the Geiger–Marsden–Rutherford experiment, almost all alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil. What does this show?
options: Most of the atom is empty space
why: Undeflected particles met nothing, so the atom is mostly empty. The positive charge of the nucleus is shown by the few large deflections, not by the straight-through ones.

q: How many neutrons are in a nucleus of $^{56}_{26}\text{Fe}$?
why: Neutron number = nucleon number − proton number = 56 − 26 = 30.

q: An electron in an atom falls from the −1.6 eV level to the −4.1 eV level. What is the energy of the emitted photon?
why: The photon carries the difference between the levels: −1.6 − (−4.1) = 2.5 eV. Adding the magnitudes (5.7 eV) is the common slip.

q: What causes the dark lines in the spectrum of light from a star?
options: Atoms in cooler gas absorbing photons of particular energies
Atoms in the star emitting photons at those wavelengths
Diffraction of the light on its way to Earth
The star being too cool to emit those wavelengths
why: Atoms in the cooler outer gas absorb only photons whose energy matches a gap between their energy levels, so those wavelengths are missing. Emission gives bright lines, not dark ones.

q: Nucleus X has nucleon number 216 and nucleus Y has nucleon number 8. The radius of X is how many times the radius of Y?
In a head-on scattering experiment, the kinetic energy of the alpha particles is doubled. What happens to the distance of closest approach?
options: It falls by a factor of $\sqrt{2}$
why: All the kinetic energy becomes electric potential energy, $E_k = \frac{kQq}{d}$, so $d \propto 1/E_k$ and it halves. The force is inverse-square, but the potential energy is only $1/d$.

q: Light above the threshold frequency shines on a metal. Its intensity is increased at the same frequency. What happens?
options: The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons increases
More photoelectrons are emitted per second, with the same maximum kinetic energy
Photoelectrons take less time to be emitted
why: Higher intensity means more photons per second, so more electrons are released, but each photon still has energy $hf$, so $E_{\max}$ is unchanged.

q: Photons of energy 5.0 eV fall on a metal with work function 2.2 eV. What is the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons, in eV?
Which observation of the photoelectric effect cannot be explained by the classical wave model of light?
options: No electrons are emitted below a threshold frequency, however bright the light
Electrons are emitted from the metal surface
The current increases when the light is made brighter
why: In the wave model, bright enough light of any frequency should eventually give electrons enough energy. A threshold frequency only makes sense if energy comes in packets $hf$.

q: An electron and a proton move at the same speed (much less than $c$). Which has the longer de Broglie wavelength?
options: It depends on the sign of the charge
why: $\lambda = h/p$ and the electron's smaller mass gives it a smaller momentum at the same speed, so its wavelength is longer. Charge plays no part.

q: A particle has momentum $6.63 \times 10^{-24}\ \text{kg m s}^{-1}$. What is its de Broglie wavelength, in nm?
In Compton scattering, at which scattering angle is the increase in the photon's wavelength greatest?
why: $\Delta\lambda = \frac{h}{m_e c}(1 - \cos\theta)$ is largest when $\cos\theta = -1$, so at 180° (photon scattered straight back). At 90° the shift is only half the maximum.

q: A sample has an activity of 800 Bq. Its half-life is 3 days. What is its activity after 9 days, in Bq?
why: 9 days is 3 half-lives: 800 → 400 → 200 → 100 Bq.

q: What happens to the proton number $Z$ and nucleon number $A$ of a nucleus in $\beta^-$ decay?
why: A neutron becomes a proton (plus an electron and an antineutrino), so $Z$ rises by 1 and $A$ stays the same. $Z$ decreasing by 1 is $\beta^+$ decay.

q: Which of these nuclei has the greatest binding energy per nucleon?
why: The binding energy per nucleon curve peaks near $A = 56$. Uranium has the greatest total binding energy, but less per nucleon.

q: A detector reads 150 counts per minute near a source; the background is 30 counts per minute. What will it read after one half-life, in counts per minute?
why: Only the source's 120 counts per minute halves, to 60; the background stays, so the reading is 60 + 30 = 90. Halving 150 to 75 is the trap.

q: The energies of beta particles from one nuclide form a continuous spectrum. What is this evidence for?
why: Each decay releases the same energy, so a range of beta energies means another particle shares it: the (anti)neutrino. Discrete levels are shown by the line spectra of alpha and gamma.

q: A nuclide has a decay constant of $0.0693\ \text{s}^{-1}$. What is its half-life?
why: $T_{1/2} = \ln 2/\lambda = 0.693/0.0693 = 10$ s. 14 s is $1/\lambda$, forgetting the $\ln 2$.

q: What is the role of the moderator in a nuclear reactor?
options: To absorb neutrons and control the reaction rate
To transfer thermal energy to the steam generator
To stop radiation escaping from the core
To slow neutrons down so they are more likely to cause fission
why: Slow (thermal) neutrons are much more likely to be captured by uranium-235. Absorbing neutrons is the job of the control rods.

q: Why does the fission of a heavy nucleus release energy?
options: The products have a greater binding energy per nucleon
The products have a greater total mass
The neutrons released carry away nucleons
The products have a smaller binding energy per nucleon
why: The products are more tightly bound, so their total mass is less than the reactants'; the mass difference is released as energy.
Nucleon number is conserved: 1 + 235 = 140 + 94 + $x$, so $x = 2$. Don't forget the incoming neutron.

q: In one fission event the mass decreases by 0.20 u. How much energy is released, in MeV?
why: 1 u is equivalent to 931.5 MeV, so 0.20 × 931.5 ≈ 186 MeV.

q: For a reactor to run at steady power, how many neutrons from each fission must, on average, go on to cause another fission?
why: Exactly one keeps the chain reaction steady. More than one makes the rate grow; the control rods absorb the extra neutrons.

q: Fission products are usually neutron-rich. By which process do they most often decay?
why: Too many neutrons: in $\beta^-$ decay a neutron turns into a proton, moving the nucleus towards stability. $\beta^+$ decay is for proton-rich nuclei.

q: What keeps a main-sequence star stable in size?
options: Outward thermal and radiation pressure balancing inward gravity
The strong force holding the star together
Gravity being balanced by magnetic forces
why: The star is in equilibrium: the pressure from hot gas and radiation pushes out as hard as gravity pulls in. The strong force acts only inside nuclei.

q: A star has a parallax angle of 0.25 arc-seconds. What is its distance, in parsecs?
Why does fusion in a star's core need a very high temperature?
options: So the nuclei can absorb photons
So the electrons are removed from the core
So the strong force becomes long-range
So nuclei move fast enough to overcome their electric repulsion
why: Nuclei must get close enough for the strong force to act, which means overcoming the repulsion between positive charges. High density then makes such collisions frequent.

q: A star is very hot but has a very low luminosity. What type of star is it?
why: Hot but dim means a very small surface area: a white dwarf, bottom left of the HR diagram. Giants are cool and bright.

q: A star has the same surface temperature as the Sun but 100 times its luminosity. Its radius is how many times the Sun's radius?
why: $L = \sigma 4\pi R^2 T^4$, so at the same $T$, $R \propto \sqrt{L}$: $\sqrt{100} = 10$.

q: How is a main-sequence star of 20 solar masses most likely to end?
options: As a white dwarf, after a planetary nebula
As a neutron star or black hole, after a supernova
As a red giant that never changes
It stays on the main sequence for ever
why: Very massive stars become supergiants and explode as supernovae, leaving a neutron star or black hole. White dwarfs are the end point for stars like the Sun.
